name: sentence-gold-biomedical-1
description: 20 hand-written biomedical/scholarly passages (#318 P2), not copied from any corpus. Each passage's text is its sentences joined by one space; `sentences` are the expected sentence units, in order. `groups` names the SENTENCE_ABBREVIATIONS groups (or negative cases) the passage covers. A change to a passage is a new fixture name, never an edit in place.

sentences: Dr. Smith and Prof. Tanaka collected the samples with Mr. Okafor at the clinic.
The analysis was performed by J. A. Rivera, Ph.D., and K. Lee, M.D., at St. Jude.
Both authors approved the final version.
Hoffmann et al. reported a similar effect in a larger cohort.
Unlike Kronmal et al. who studied adults, we enrolled children.
The difference was not significant.
Opportunistic infections (e.g. tuberculosis) were excluded, i.e. only primary cases were analysed.
Other exclusions, viz. pregnancy and dialysis, are listed elsewhere, cf. the protocol.
Recruitment closed in 2019.
Mortality was 12% vs. 18% in the two arms, and enrolment took ca. 14 months.
Secondary outcomes (length of stay, readmission, etc.) are reported in the appendix.
No adverse events were attributed to the intervention.
Survivin was absent from the mesenchyme (Fig. 4A).
Its expression rose in later stages, as Figs. 5 and 6 show.
The pattern was reproducible.
Expression levels are summarised in Fig. 2.
The results were consistent across replicates.
Baseline characteristics are given in Tab. 1 and the model in Eq. 3 of Ref. 12.
Parameters were fitted as in Eqs. 4 and 5 (see Refs. 7 and 9).
Fit quality was good.
Primer sequences are listed in Suppl. Table S2.
The method follows Ch. 4 of the manual, Vol. 2, pp. 113-120.
The antibody was purchased from Abcam (cat. no. 12345) and used at 1:500.
Cells were incubated at a final conc. of approx. 5 uM for 2 days.
The mol. wt. of the purified protein was 42 kDa.
Incubation temp. was held constant.
The dose was 3 mg/kg.
The next cohort received twice that dose.
Cells were then washed for 5 min.
Imaging followed immediately.
Mice were injected i.v. with the vector and received the drug i.p. on day 3.
Patients took 200 mg p.o. b.i.d. for two weeks.
Compliance was monitored by pill count.
Isolates of Bacillus sp. strain KR-1 and Streptococcus spp. were obtained from the culture collection.
Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhi was grown overnight.
Escherichia coli str. K-12 served as control.
E. coli K-12 and S. enterica were grown in LB medium.
B. subtilis did not grow under these conditions, unlike P. aeruginosa.
Growth of C. trachomatis required host cells.
Patients were randomised to group A or group B.
3 patients withdrew before the first visit.
The assay was first described in Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. in 2001.
A refinement appeared in J. Biol. Chem. two years later.
Clinical validation was published in N. Engl. J. Med. and Ann. Intern. Med.
Reagents were purchased from Sigma Chemical Co. (St. Louis, MO) and from Wako Ltd. in Osaka.
Sequencing was done by the Dept. of Genetics, Univ. of Toronto, for the U.S. arm and the U.K. arm.
All data were deposited.
Samples were collected between Jan. 2018 and Sept. 2019.
A second round ran from Oct. 2020 to Dec. 2021.
No samples were lost.
Patients in arm 2. received placebo, while those in arm 1. received the active drug.
The trial was double blind.
Follow-up lasted 12 months.
Most patients presented to the ED.
Those with mild symptoms were discharged within hours.
Admissions were rare.
Dr. Smith et al. reported a 2.5-fold increase (p < 0.05).
Fig. 2 shows the effect in vivo, i.e. in mice infected with S. aureus at approx. 10^6 CFU.
The U.S. cohort was smaller.
Why the effect was weaker there is unclear!
Further work is needed?
